query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled tungsten addition (≈10 at.%) into the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high‐entropy alloy—with a subsequent aging treatment designed to promote a fine dispersion of tungsten-rich precipitates—will enhance the dynamic strain hardening and uniform deformability and delay adiabatic shear localization under high strain‐rate (adiabatic) deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high‐entropy alloy with quasi‐static properties: 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain.
generation.intervention: Substitutionally add roughly 10 at.% tungsten (by adjusting the alloy’s elemental ratios, e.g. partially replacing Ta) and subject the alloy to a solution treatment and subsequent aging heat treatment to precipitate fine, coherent tungsten‐rich secondary phases.
generation.conditions: Dynamic compression experiments conducted at room temperature under adiabatic conditions with strain rates in the range of approximately 1300 s⁻¹ to 2100 s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: The finely dispersed tungsten-rich precipitates within the BCC matrix act as strong obstacles to dislocation motion and help distribute local strain, thereby enhancing strain hardening and delaying the onset of shear localization.
generation.mechanism: W additions increase the melting point and introduce precipitate obstacles that impede dislocation glide, mitigating adiabatic thermal softening. This increased dislocation resistance under high strain rates leads to enhanced strain hardening and a more uniform deformation before catastrophic failure via adiabatic shear banding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the tungsten-modified alloy is expected to achieve higher dynamic yield and compressive strengths (exceeding 786 MPa and 1314 MPa, respectively), a higher uniform strain to fracture (beyond 13.5%), increased strain-hardening rate, better resistance to adiabatic shear localization, and greater impact-induced energy absorption.
generation.baseline: HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA exhibiting quasi-static mechanical properties of 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain.
generation.boundary: The enhanced performance is predicted to apply under high strain-rate, adiabatic loading conditions (approximately 1300 s⁻¹ to 2100 s⁻¹ at room temperature); results outside this regime (e.g. at very low strain rates or significantly elevated temperatures) may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements (e.g. exact percentage increases in strength and ductility) and the optimal tungsten content/aging parameters remain uncertain until experimental validation is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of samples: (1) the baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy and (2) the tungsten-modified alloy (with ≈10 at.% tungsten addition and identical thermomechanical processing including solution treatment and aging). Subject both sets to dynamic compression tests using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar under controlled, adiabatic conditions at strain rates of ~1300 s⁻¹ and ~2100 s⁻¹.
measurements: Uniform fracture strain (measured by deformation before localization)
Strain-hardening rate (evaluated from the stress–strain response)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM/SEM to assess tungsten-rich precipitate dispersion and evidence of shear banding)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements—in terms of enhanced dynamic strength, increased uniform deformability (higher strain to fracture), higher strain-hardening rate, and reduced occurrence or severity of adiabatic shear localization—compared to the baseline alloy under the designated high strain-rate conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Effect of W Element on Mechanical Properties and Microstructure
cited_evidence.text: The quasi-static compressive stress–strain curves of the alloys with varying W contents are presented in Figure 2a. For the W0 alloy, the yield strength (σYS) and the ultimate strength (σUS) are approximately 1620 MPa and 1810 MPa, respectively, with an elongation of ~22%. Serrated steps observed in the stress–strain curve of W0 suggest a susceptibility to plastic instability. The introduction of W into the alloy preserves the high yield strength while significantly improving both fracture strength and fracture strain []. For example, the W13 alloy demonstrates a yield strength of 1650 MPa, along with an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa and a fracture strain of 32%. Figure 2b presents the dynamic engineering stress–strain curves of alloys with varying W contents, tested at high strain rates (2000 s−1) and at room temperature. Under dynamic conditions, the yield strength of each alloy is significantly enhanced compared with the quasi-static conditions. Notably, while the W0 and W8 alloys exhibit poor dynamic plasticity with elongations below 10%, the W13 and W18 alloys demonstrate superior dynamic mechanical properties, achieving ultra-high dynamic yield strengths (exceeding 2200 MPa)

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity.
